questions.q: What does the threshold theorem state?
options: There exists a physical error rate p_th such that below it, increasing code distance exponentially suppresses the logical error rate; at or above it, increasing distance does not help
Every quantum code has exactly the same threshold value, regardless of its structure
Logical error rate always decreases as distance increases, with no threshold involved
The threshold theorem only applies to classical repetition codes, not quantum codes
questions.explain: The threshold theorem's precise claim is the existence of a below/above-threshold distinction in how distance affects logical error rate -- the mathematical basis for believing scalable quantum error correction is possible.

questions.q: Using the illustrative scaling table (p_th=0.01, p=0.001), what is the computed logical error suppression factor at distance d=9?
options: Approximately 1.000 x 10^-5
Approximately 1.000 x 10^-2
Approximately 1.000 x 10^-9
Exactly 0, meaning zero logical errors
questions.explain: With exponent (9+1)/2=5, (0.001/0.01)^5 = 0.1^5 = 1.000x10^-5, matching the verified table.

questions.q: What happens to the exponential suppression behavior if the physical error rate p is at or above the threshold p_th?
options: The suppression effect inverts -- increasing distance no longer shrinks the logical error rate, and can make it worse by adding more qubits without compensating benefit
The suppression effect becomes even stronger than below threshold
Nothing changes; the formula behaves identically above and below threshold
The code becomes immune to all errors regardless of distance
questions.explain: Above threshold, (p/p_th) is >= 1, so raising it to a higher power no longer shrinks the result -- it stays flat or grows, meaning scaling up can actively hurt rather than help.

questions.q: What does the lesson say is proven and well-established versus what remains empirical and hardware-specific?
options: The existence of a threshold for code families like the surface code is proven; the actual numerical threshold value and whether specific real hardware operates below it is empirical and still evolving
Both the existence of a threshold and its exact numerical value for every real device are fully settled facts
Nothing about the threshold theorem has been proven; it remains purely speculative
The threshold theorem has been experimentally disproven for all known hardware platforms
questions.explain: The lesson draws an explicit, honest line: the theoretical existence of a threshold is established, but specific real-hardware threshold values and whether a device operates below them are empirical questions the course does not claim are settled.

questions.q: Combining the threshold table with the previous lesson's qubit-cost table, going from d=7 to d=15 costs roughly 4.6x more physical qubits. What suppression benefit does the illustrative scaling show for that same jump?
options: Roughly 10,000x better logical error suppression (10^-4 down to 10^-8)
Exactly the same suppression benefit, no improvement at all
A worse logical error rate than at d=7
Only a 2x improvement in suppression
questions.explain: The illustrative table shows 10^-4 at d=7 and 10^-8 at d=15, a 10,000x improvement in suppression, for only a 4.6x qubit-cost increase -- the favorable trade that justifies the threshold theorem's practical importance.
